title: What slander does inside
hook: slander darkens the one who speaks it (Sukhmani 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harm of slander, and your line: slander harms the slanderer. Did you let one unkind conversation pass in silence? Today we look inside the one who speaks, and at what to put there instead. Day four hundred eighty-eight.
screen: `THE HARM OF SLANDER — SLANDER HARMS THE SLANDERER.`

segments.voice: Ever notice how a complaint grows when you tell it? The first time, it's a small thing your brother said. By the third retelling, it has a beginning, a middle and a villain. You've rehearsed it so often you can feel it in your jaw. The brother has long since forgotten. You haven't, because you've been carrying it around and polishing it. Slander works like that on the inside. It doesn't stay out there, in the story. It moves in. Today: what slander does inside the one who speaks it, and the one small word Sikhs put in its place.
screen: `A COMPLAINT GROWS EACH TELLING.` → `YOU FEEL IT IN YOUR JAW.` → `SLANDER MOVES IN.`

segments.voice: Among the costs in the thirteenth ashtpadi, one goes deeper than the rest. Through slandering the holy, the text says, the mind becomes maleen: dirty, stained, like cloth dipped in mud. It's an inside cost. Not a punishment arriving later, but a change happening right now, in the person speaking. Every time you rehearse someone's faults, you're the one marinating in them. The Guru Granth Sahib has a famous picture of this from the other side. The poet-saint Kabir, whose hymns sit in the scripture beside the Gurus', says something startling: let people slander me; the slanderer is actually my helper. Why? Because, in Kabir's image, the slanderer washes my dirty clothes for me. My faults move off me and onto their tongue. It's funny and a little unsettling, and it says the same thing as Sukhmani: the dirt ends up with the one who talks. So what goes in its place? Sikhs have an answer they say every day. The Ardas, the standing prayer said at the end of so much of Sikh worship, closes with a line that ends sarbat da bhalaa. The good of all. The well-being of everyone, with no list of exceptions. Not my family, my side, the people I like: sarbat, all. People who say Ardas daily are, every day, wishing well to the very people they might be tempted to slander. That's the swap. Not just stopping the unkind word, which leaves an empty space. Filling the space with a blessing. A stained cloth doesn't get clean by being left alone. It gets clean by being washed.
screen: `THE MIND MADE MALEEN: STAINED.` · `KABIR: THE SLANDERER WASHES ME.` · `ARDAS: SARBAT DA BHALAA.` · `FILL THE SPACE WITH A BLESSING.` · then, large: `BLESS INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: swap one criticism for a blessing. Bring to mind one person you've been criticizing lately, out loud or just in your head. Notice the complaint, the polished story. Now set it down. In its place, wish them one plain good thing: that they sleep well tonight, that their work goes right, that they're less worried than they seem. If you pray, you can hold them inside sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all. The bell holds the time.
What slander does inside. It stains the speaker's own mind, maleen; and the Ardas puts sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all, in its place.
Your line: bless instead. Today, every time you catch a criticism forming about someone, follow it with one silent good wish for them. Day four hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs end the Ardas, the standing prayer said at the close of daily worship and many gatherings, with a line asking for sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all; Sukhmani's thirteenth ashtpadi names slander's inner stain.

the mind of the one speaking becomes maleen, stained.

fork.setup: you've stopped yourself from criticizing someone. there's an empty space where the complaint was. what does this lesson put there?
fork.reveal: a blessing. Sikhs pray daily for sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all; a stained cloth gets clean by washing, not by waiting.

original.note: Punjabi: sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all, the closing words of the Ardas.

trapdoor: what you thought: if I keep the complaint in my head, no harm done.
what it means: slander stains the speaker's mind first; the remedy is not only silence but blessing.
what a scholar hears: Sukhmani 13's mat hoi maleen sits beside Kabir's hymn in which the nindak washes the devotee's clothes, two images of where the dirt goes.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 13 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279–280)

notes: Line in ashtpadi 13 that the slanderer's mind becomes maleen: confirm wording and stanza.
Kabir's hymn (nindau nindau mo kau log nindau; the nindak washes my clothes) placed in Raag Gauri at Ang 339: confirm Ang and the paraphrase.
Ardas closing (Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhalaa): confirm transliteration and Gurmukhi ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ.
